listening.title: The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear forever
listening.topic: The ancient glaciers of Papua's Sudirman Range are vanishing due to climate change, threatening both scientific knowledge and indigenous spiritual heritage.
listening.topic_zh: 印尼巴布亞蘇迪曼山脈的古老冰川正因氣候變化而消融，威脅到科學知識與原住民精神文化遺產。
listening.transcript_excerpt: High in the mountains of Papua, Indonesia, something extraordinary is disappearing. For centuries, peaks near the equator have been capped with what local people call 'eternal snow' — a phenomenon so rare in the tropics that scientists and spiritual leaders alike have marvelled at its existence. But climate change is now erasing this ancient ice at a staggering pace. A hundred years ago, all four major peaks of the Sudirman Range were blanketed in permanent snow and ice. Today, only tiny patches survive near Puncak Jaya, also known as Carstensz Pyramid. Researchers estimate these last remnants will vanish entirely within just a year or two. The scale of the loss is almost incomprehensible. Glacier cover has plummeted from nearly 1,900 hectares in the nineteenth century to a mere 16 hectares today. For scientists like Czech glacier ecologist Marie Šabacká, who rushed to the site last March hoping to be among the last researchers to study the ice, the situation carries a deep sense of injustice. 'There is a profound unfairness in this,' she says. Papua's glaciers are uniquely isolated, separated from other glacier systems by thousands of kilometres. They represent the last tropical ice between the Andes and the Himalayas. Crucially, ice cores extracted from these slopes contain an irreplaceable record of Earth's atmospheric history, offering clues about the behaviour of the Pacific Ocean's warmest waters. As the ice melts, that archive is being lost forever — before scientists have had adequate time to study it.

vocabulary.definition: a large, slow-moving mass of ice formed from compacted snow over many years, found in high mountains or polar regions
vocabulary.definition_zh: 冰川；由多年積雪壓縮而成的大型緩慢移動冰體，存在於高山或極地地區
vocabulary.example: The glacier had retreated by several kilometres over the past fifty years due to rising global temperatures.

vocabulary.definition: the central or most important point of something, often used metaphorically to indicate a focal point of activity or significance
vocabulary.definition_zh: 核心；最重要的中心點，常用於比喻某事物的焦點或重要之處
vocabulary.example: The city became the epicentre of the environmental movement after the disaster drew international attention.

vocabulary.definition: very deep, intense, or far-reaching in effect or significance; showing great insight or seriousness
vocabulary.definition_zh: 深刻的；深遠的；影響重大的，表示深度的嚴肅性或重要性
vocabulary.example: The loss of the ancient forest had a profound impact on the indigenous communities who had lived there for generations.

vocabulary.definition: a cylindrical sample drilled from a glacier or ice sheet, used by scientists to study past atmospheric conditions and climate history
vocabulary.definition_zh: 冰芯；從冰川或冰蓋中鑽取的圓柱形樣本，科學家用來研究過去的大氣狀況和氣候歷史
vocabulary.example: By analysing the ice core, researchers were able to reconstruct temperature patterns from thousands of years ago.

vocabulary.definition: a collection of historical records or evidence preserved for future reference; a repository of accumulated information
vocabulary.definition_zh: 檔案；史料庫；為未來參考而保存的歷史記錄或證據的集合
vocabulary.example: The melting permafrost threatened to destroy a biological archive that scientists had only begun to understand.

questions.q: How much glacier cover remains near Puncak Jaya today compared to the nineteenth century?
options: A: Approximately 190 hectares remain out of an original 1,900 hectares
B: Approximately 16 hectares remain out of an original 1,900 hectares
C: Approximately 160 hectares remain out of an original 1,900 hectares
D: Approximately 60 hectares remain out of an original 600 hectares
questions.explanation: The passage clearly states that glacier cover has shrunk from nearly 1,900 hectares in the 19th century to about 16 hectares today, making B the only accurate figure.

questions.q: Why does Marie Šabacká describe the situation as having 'a profound unfairness'?
options: A: Because wealthy nations caused climate change but Papua bears the spiritual loss
B: Because scientists were denied permission to study the glaciers in time
C: Because the glaciers are disappearing before scientists have had adequate time to study them
D: Because indigenous communities receive no financial compensation for their loss
questions.explanation: The text states she expresses profound unfairness because the scientific archive contained in the ice cores is vanishing before researchers have had time to fully study it, not primarily for political or financial reasons.

questions.q: What makes Papua's glaciers scientifically unique according to the passage?
options: A: They are the oldest glaciers on Earth and contain the most complete climate records
B: They are isolated from other glacier systems by thousands of kilometres and represent the last tropical ice between the Andes and Himalayas
C: They are located exactly on the equator, which makes them geologically impossible to explain
D: They are the largest glaciers in the Southern Hemisphere and supply fresh water to the Pacific
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly notes that Papua's glaciers are unique because they are separated from other systems by thousands of kilometres and are the last remaining tropical ice between the Andes and the Himalayas.

reading.title: The Disappearing Glaciers of Papua: Climate Loss at the Equator
reading.passage:
The Sudirman Range in Papua, Indonesia, represents one of the most climatologically anomalous landscapes on Earth. Situated close to the equator, its peaks once harboured permanent glaciers — a phenomenon that has fascinated scientists and inspired reverence among indigenous Papuan communities for centuries. However, accelerating climate change has brought this remarkable feature to the brink of extinction, raising urgent questions about scientific heritage, cultural identity, and environmental justice.

A century ago, all four principal summits of the Sudirman Range were blanketed in permanent snow and ice extending across approximately 1,900 hectares. Today, that coverage has contracted to a mere 16 hectares, confined almost entirely to the upper slopes of Puncak Jaya, which, at 4,884 metres, is the highest peak in Southeast Asia and Oceania. Glaciologists estimate that these final remnants will disappear entirely within one to two years, rendering the Sudirman Range the latest casualty of global warming's disproportionate impact on equatorial environments.

The scientific significance of Papua's glaciers extends beyond their geographical novelty. Ice cores extracted from Puncak Jaya's slopes serve as a cryospheric archive, preserving detailed records of atmospheric composition, precipitation patterns, and temperature fluctuations spanning millennia. These records are particularly valuable for understanding the behaviour of the Western Pacific Warm Pool, a body of exceptionally warm ocean water that influences weather systems across the Indo-Pacific region. As the ice disappears, so too does this irreplaceable data reservoir.

For many Papuans, the loss carries an equally profound cultural dimension. The snow-capped mountains occupy a central place in indigenous cosmology, functioning as a sacred axis connecting the physical and spiritual realms. Activists have compared their significance to that of Mecca for Muslims or the Vatican for Catholics — sacred spaces whose desecration represents an existential wound to community identity. The intersection of scientific loss and cultural grief makes Papua's glacial retreat a uniquely poignant symbol of the broader climate crisis.

questions.statement: A century ago, the Sudirman Range had permanent snow and ice on all four of its major peaks.
questions.explanation: The passage states explicitly that a century ago all four principal summits were blanketed in permanent snow and ice, confirming this statement as True.

questions.statement: Puncak Jaya is the highest mountain peak in the entire Asian continent.
questions.explanation: The passage describes Puncak Jaya as the highest peak in Southeast Asia and Oceania, not the entire Asian continent, making this statement False.

questions.statement: The Papuan government has introduced legislation specifically to protect the remaining glaciers from further melting.
questions.explanation: The passage makes no mention of any governmental legislation or policy responses aimed at protecting the glaciers; this information is entirely absent from the text.

questions.q: According to the passage, what is the primary scientific value of the ice cores extracted from Puncak Jaya?
options: A: They allow scientists to measure the current speed of glacial retreat across the tropics
B: They preserve records of atmospheric conditions, precipitation, and temperature changes over thousands of years
C: They provide biological samples of ancient plant and animal species unique to Papua
D: They enable researchers to predict future volcanic activity beneath the Sudirman Range
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly states that ice cores serve as a cryospheric archive preserving records of atmospheric composition, precipitation patterns, and temperature fluctuations spanning millennia, matching option B precisely.

speaking.topic: Describe a natural place or landscape that is important to you or to a community you know about.
speaking.topic_zh: 描述一個對你或你所了解的社群具有重要意義的自然地方或景觀。

part2.cue_card:
Describe a natural place or landscape that is important to you or to a community you know about.

You should say:
• What the place is and where it is located
• Why it is significant — scientifically, culturally, or spiritually
• What threats, if any, this place currently faces
• And explain how you feel about the possibility of this place changing or disappearing forever.

You will have one minute to prepare and should speak for one to two minutes.
band_tips: Use vivid, precise language to paint a sensory picture of the landscape — describe colours, textures, and atmosphere rather than simply listing facts, as this demonstrates lexical sophistication at Band 7 and above.

Organise your response with a clear narrative arc: introduce the place, build its significance, then shift emotionally toward the threat it faces. This structured progression signals coherence and cohesion to the examiner.

Incorporate advanced vocabulary naturally — words such as 'irreplaceable', 'profound', 'epicentre of cultural identity', or 'existential loss' will elevate your response without sounding rehearsed if woven into genuine reflection.

part3.q: Do you think governments have a responsibility to protect natural landscapes, even when doing so conflicts with economic development goals?
part3.q_zh: 您認為政府有責任保護自然景觀嗎，即使這樣做與經濟發展目標相衝突？
key_points: Governments bear a custodial duty to preserve environments for future generations, as natural heritage cannot be recreated once destroyed
Economic and environmental goals can often be reconciled through sustainable development frameworks such as eco-tourism or green infrastructure
However, in developing nations, short-term economic pressures frequently override long-term environmental stewardship, suggesting that international financial support mechanisms are essential

part3.q: How significant is the loss of a natural place to the cultural identity of an indigenous community, and how does this compare to other forms of cultural loss?
part3.q_zh: 自然地方的消失對原住民社群的文化認同有多重要？這與其他形式的文化喪失相比如何？
key_points: For many indigenous peoples, landscapes are not merely physical spaces but are embedded in spiritual practice, oral history, and cosmological belief, making their loss categorically different from, say, the loss of a language or artefact
Unlike a language, which can be documented or revived, a physical landscape once destroyed cannot be reconstructed, giving landscape loss a uniquely irreversible character

This form of loss intersects with broader issues of environmental justice, since indigenous communities rarely contribute significantly to the carbon emissions driving climate change yet bear its most severe consequences

part3.q: Should scientists prioritise studying endangered natural sites before they disappear, even if gaining access is logistically difficult or expensive?
part3.q_zh: 科學家是否應該優先研究瀕危自然地點，即使取得研究機會在後勤上很困難或費用高昂？
key_points: The urgency argument is compelling — once a glacier, coral reef, or rainforest disappears, the data it holds is permanently lost, making immediate research a matter of scientific necessity
Resource allocation is inevitably constrained, and prioritising endangered sites may require diverting funding from other valuable research areas, raising questions of opportunity cost

International scientific collaboration and dedicated emergency funding mechanisms could allow endangered site research to proceed without disproportionately burdening individual institutions or nations

part3.q: To what extent do you think ordinary people in developed countries are aware of the environmental changes happening in remote parts of the world, and does this awareness matter?
part3.q_zh: 您認為發達國家的普通民眾在多大程度上意識到世界偏遠地區正在發生的環境變化？這種意識重要嗎？
key_points: Media coverage of remote environmental events is typically sporadic and brief, meaning public awareness tends to be shallow and easily displaced by domestic news cycles
However, awareness does matter because consumer behaviour, voting patterns, and public pressure on corporations are all influenced by the public's understanding of global environmental consequences

Digital media and social platforms have created new opportunities for remote communities to share their experiences directly with global audiences, potentially bypassing traditional media gatekeepers and building genuine empathy

writing.task2_question: Ancient glaciers and other unique natural formations are disappearing due to climate change, taking with them irreplaceable scientific data and cultural heritage. Some people argue that the international community has a collective moral obligation to prevent such losses, while others believe individual nations must take primary responsibility for protecting their own environments. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
writing.task2_question_zh: 由於氣候變化，古老的冰川和其他獨特的自然景觀正在消失，帶走了不可替代的科學數據和文化遺產。一些人認為國際社會有集體道德義務防止此類損失，而另一些人則認為各個國家必須對保護本國環境承擔主要責任。討論兩種觀點並給出您自己的意見。

useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use when arguing that one party suffers consequences that exceed their degree of responsibility or contribution to a problem
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 當論述某一方所承受的後果超出其對問題的責任或貢獻程度時使用
useful_phrases.example: It is deeply inequitable that Papua bears a disproportionate burden of climate consequences despite contributing negligibly to global carbon emissions.

useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use to emphasise that once a certain point is crossed — environmental, biological, or social — the situation cannot be undone
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 用來強調一旦超過某個臨界點（環境、生物或社會），情況就無法挽回
useful_phrases.example: Scientists warn that many glacial systems are approaching an irreversible threshold beyond which complete melt becomes inevitable regardless of future emission reductions.

useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use when arguing that an issue has implications too broad or interconnected to be addressed by a single nation alone
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 當論述某一問題的影響範圍過於廣泛或相互關聯，無法由單一國家單獨解決時使用
useful_phrases.example: Climate change is a crisis that fundamentally transcends national borders, demanding coordinated international responses rather than isolated domestic policies.

useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use when discussing the duty of governments, organisations, or generations to preserve something valuable for future users or inheritors
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 討論政府、組織或世代有責任為未來的使用者或繼承者保存有價值事物時使用
useful_phrases.example: Wealthier nations that have historically driven industrialisation must acknowledge their custodial responsibility toward the global environments their emissions have damaged.

useful_phrases.phrase: the convergence of scientific and cultural loss
useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use to introduce or summarise arguments that combine two distinct but related forms of damage caused by a single phenomenon
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 用於介紹或總結由單一現象引起的兩種不同但相關的損害形式
useful_phrases.example: The melting of Papua's glaciers exemplifies the convergence of scientific and cultural loss, as both priceless climate data and indigenous spiritual heritage are erased simultaneously.

outline.intro: Open with a vivid reference to the disappearing glaciers of Papua as a concrete example of the broader dilemma. Paraphrase the question to establish that both collective international obligation and national sovereignty arguments have merit, then state a clear thesis: while nations hold primary administrative responsibility, the moral and practical dimensions of climate-driven environmental loss necessitate coordinated international action.
outline.body1: Present the case for national responsibility: sovereignty principles dictate that individual states are the primary stewards of their own territories; effective governance, local knowledge, and direct accountability mean national governments are best placed to implement protective measures; over-reliance on international bodies can create diffusion of responsibility where no single actor feels truly accountable.
outline.body2: Counter with the stronger argument for international collective obligation: climate change is caused overwhelmingly by emissions from industrialised nations, creating a moral debt toward vulnerable countries like Papua; unique natural and cultural heritage belongs to humanity as a whole, not merely to the nation where it is located; international frameworks such as the Paris Agreement and UNESCO World Heritage mechanisms demonstrate that collective action is both possible and necessary when threats exceed the capacity of individual states.
outline.conclusion: Restate the thesis by affirming that national governments must serve as primary implementers, but that the moral responsibility — and the financial and technical resources — must be shared internationally. Close with a forward-looking statement emphasising that the imminent loss of Papua's glaciers should serve as a catalyst for more ambitious and equitable global climate cooperation.
